Editor’s NotesBy Steve Fairbairn
Ed Pretty kicks off this month’s newsletter with the
monthly Tech Talk article with a discussion about
lathe speed. Elsewhere in the newsletter he recaps
his Sharpening presentation from last month’s
monthly meeting.
John Hammond recaps his February presentation
on drawing Celtic knots with step-by-step instructions. Sheila Balzer returns with her monthly column chronicling her journey as a new turner.
This month’s Member Profile features Dan Breck.
You’re probably tired of hearing me say it but, we
do need your articles/musings for our club’s newsletter. I highly encourage those who have never
submitted an article to give it a try, even if it’s just
a tip or hint about something that makes your life
easier in your workspace.
Steve
Presidential RamblingsBy Steve Hansen
A hearty thank you to Matt Lo for joining our A/V
team. Matt also donated a large stash of wood to
the club, some of which will be used in our Spindle
Classes. Thanks to Scott Belway for his donation of
hardwood flooring cut-offs – they look quite suitable for pens and segmented work.
A kind reminder to everyone to please check your
DVD library for any Guild volumes and please return them. We are currently holding your $10 deposit on each volume so there’s an added incentive
to dig through your collection.
Art Liestman makes headlines… again! Art’s
“Village” was selected and recognized by the AAW
and the Professional Outreach Program for pieces
featured in the Themed Member Exhibition and
the Instant Gallery. Well done Art! While on the
topic of Symposia, next year’s event is in Portland,
just a hop skip and a jump down I5 or Amtrak! Six
years ago, in Portland, there were about 2 dozen
members attended from our Guild plus many from
the Fraser Valley Guild.
Don’t forget, July 23 is the Guild Potluck Picnic. The
Guild will provide tables, a grill, “something to
grill”. Please bring a small side-dish or dessert to
share. As in the past it’s a fun afternoon of games,
tours, and a small auction!
September’s
challenge
is
“embellishment”.
Steve

Tech TalkBy Ed Pretty
Turning Speed
I have been asked many times what speed (rpm) I
am turning a particular item at or about the subject
of turning speed in general. I’m sorry to say that I
rarely, if ever, check the speed I am turning at because I’m so used to turning at what I feel is an appropriate speed that I never look. Like everything
else in woodturning: Goldilocks speed.
A day or two prior to the Zoom meeting I happened to see a post on the Canadian Woodturners
FB page relating to that subject. It was apparently
provided by Allan Batty (no proof of that) so, although
Allan
is
certainly
a
credible
(understatement) source, I have to question part of
the information.
The chart attached to the post lists speeds in miles
per hour (rim speed, I assume) and the magic number is 45 mph. It seems that anything that comes
off the lathe under 45 mph will go down while anything above 45 mph will fly up. Considering there
are myriad other physical influences, my Spidey
sense (and Newton’s Third Law of Motion) tells me
that sounds highly suspicious (BS is more like it).
The point of the whole thing is to keep your rim
speed below 45 mph which is wise, judging from
the numbers. That being said, from the chart a 16”
bowl turning at 950 rpm is certainly pretty quick
and I doubt I would ever turn that fast even if everything was in balance, no cracks, sharp tool, securely mounted, etc., etc. Although I question the
upward and downward reactions, the speeds listed
give a good example of three spindle speeds that
seem too high for the listed diameters.
Because I have been asked about turning speeds so
many times, this motivated me to go out to the
shop and put various diameters of wood in the
lathe and turned the speed up to what I felt comfortable turning at. In listing these speeds I am assuming optimum conditions: secure work holding,
sound and balanced wood, sharp tools and proper
technique. Anytime there is an imbalance, cracks,
significant tool overhang or any other condition
that is at all suspect, I opt for a slower speed. Also,
consider that I am reasonably experienced and
have turned at these speeds before, having worked
up to them over time.
In my own chart below, I listed the “Batty” speeds
in white and my rpm and rim speeds in yellow. At
the small diameter end, my lathe only goes to 3600
rpm so would turn very small diameters (i.e. pens
or bobbins) faster if it was possible. You will note
that I wouldn’t turn a 16” bowl anywhere close to
950 rpm.
This was interesting because in doing the math on
the rim speed, it seems that I end up turning with a
rim speed somewhere between 2000 to just over
3000 feet per minute range no matter what diameter I am turning. I never knew that before. This is

certainly not a definitive analysis and not for everyone.
I know there is a formula for calculating a safe
speed range (6000 ÷ diameter in inches for lowest
speed, 9000 ÷ diameter in inches for highest
speed) but I like John Jordan’s guide the best: If
you turn the lathe on and you kind of cringe at how
fast it’s going, turn it down. If you are getting beat
up because of the slow speed pounding, turn it up.
I’m not recommending anyone turn at the speeds
in my own chart, I’m only answering the perpetual
question, “How fast do you turn?”.
And for what it’s worth, since our discussion, I had
a large, staved piece break up on me at a very low
speed (22” diameter and no, I have no idea what
the speed was). I’m here to tell you that some pieces went up, the heavy one went down, and one
went all the way across the shop (I found that 4th
piece after this picture was taken). That pretty
much covered the range so it must have been turning both above and below 45 mph at the same
time. And yes, I was able to salvage the piece.
Stropping
I ended up doing a deep dive on this after our discussion because of a question during my Sharpening demo at the general meeting. Rather than write
it all down twice, check out the article on the
sharpening demo.
Wood ID
Claudia asked if anyone could help her confirm the
species of a piece of wood she has. Several suggestions were made including UBC (Forintech, which
now only caters to industry), a wood identification
app called Xylorix Pocket Wood (requires a lens for
your phone) or using a dissecting microscope
(handy to no one). Mike Moult described Koa (the
suspected species) in great detail so was probably
able to help with that information alone.
Tool rest
Steve noted that he had a tool rest that had a carbide inclusion in the casting so was unable to file it
smooth. The discussion was oriented around how
to attach a hardened rod to an existing tool rest or
to a piece of mild steel if making a tool rest. Generally, using heat (welding or brazing) to attach hardened rod to something is out since the hardness
and surface texture would be destroyed. It was
noted that there are probably epoxies available to
do the job. Speaking with Steve later, he decided to

This Month’s Cover
By David Sweet O.C.
Mary E. Elliott Award 2023
- David Sweet O.C. and Steve Fairbairn
The Canadian Botanical Association (CBA) presents
an annual award to a top Canadian botanist to
commemorate the outstanding service of one of its
members. This award is entitled the Mary E. Elliott
Award after the then President of the CBA who
died suddenly as a victim of crime in September
1976. This year’s award recipient is Dr. John H.
Markham from the University of Manitoba in Winnipeg.
One of our GVWG members, David Sweet, who
took several botany elective courses at university
as an undergrad and met top botanists working in
academia then, has been making these annual
awards for the past 15 years. David attempts to
personalize each award by adding graphics that
relate to images from the career of that year’s recipient or using a timber blank that is the subject of
the recipients’ field of study.
Dr. Markham has studied Alnus alnobetula ssp.
crispa (green alder) in Canada’s boreal forests
throughout his career with emphasis on a symbiosis that exists between nitrogen-producing bacteria
that live in alder roots and the alders.
This month’s cover photo is of the platter that David has made this month in collaboration with PastPresident Steve Fairbairn. Steve’s expertise in laser
engraving is unsurpassed, and as you can see, he
has engraved the finest of details in both the green
alder leaves and twigs, etc. and in the tiny text
along the branch. This platter is 13” (33cm) diameter and 2” (5cm) deep. It is finished with two coats
of walnut oil and six coats for WOP.

Subsequent to this discussion, I did some research
on the subject of welding hardened 4140 steel
(because I am somewhat familiar with that grade)
since Robust obviously welds their rests with what
appears to be tig welding. I found it is possible
(with pre and post heating to about 400+ degrees
F.) so have purchased the steel necessary and am
in the process of having a friend do some tig welding for me. I’ll report back later.
Finish application material
Dan noted that his neighbour is an automotive
painter and was suggesting using “shop rags” for
applying finishes like wipe on poly. Unfortunately,
he wasn’t sure of the type of material but felt it
was some type of “poly”, perhaps polypropylene.
The discussion ranged through various materials
including nylon stockings, but the main quality was
that the material be “lint free”. The discussion
went rapidly downhill after the nylon stockings
were mentioned.

They can be evenly spaced or variable spaced. This can allow fitting in the space your need the design to be in as in a border on a plate or a circle in the center of a platter.

•

Sharpening Turning ToolsBy Ed Pretty
Like woodturning, sharpening is part technical savvy and part Dark Art, so they both have a fairly
steep learning curve. Unfortunately, you can’t turn
if you don’t have sharp tools, so learning the two
go hand in hand. The good news is that we have
plenty of excellent sharpening equipment and high
-quality steel for our tools available to us.
Safety
Like any activity in our shop, safety is primary. Here
are things to consider.
a. Always wear eye protection
b. Use hearing protection over long periods (i.e.
reshaping)
c. Use breathing protection
d. DO NOT USE cracked or damaged refractory
wheels (ring test before installation or if
bumped or chipped in use)
e. Have guards in place for vitrified wheels
f. Vitrified wheels must have paper labels in place
g. DO NOT adjust tool rests while the wheels are
moving
h. Don’t grind on the sides of the wheel unless it
has been designed for that use. Normal vitrified
grindstones are not.
Steels
It’s safe to say that all the turning tools available
today are made using some grade of High Speed
Steel (HSS). Like any steel, however, quality varies
so not all HSS is the same. There is a vast number
of grades used by manufacturers with many being
excellent and a few being poor (read: noticeably
cheaper than everything else). It’s like splitting
hairs when it comes to high quality HSS so there’s
no point explaining them all here. Suffice to say
that, in general, you get what you pay for so let
that be your guide until you determine your personal preference.
Occasionally most of us have been offered some
older high carbon steel (0.8% to 1.2% carbon) tools
and my advice is to grab them. They don’t withstand the heat produced while turning as well as
HSS, but you can get them way sharper because of
the smaller crystalline structure of carbon steel and
the price is usually right. You can grind them specifically for one obscure job so they will be well
worth having.
In general, turning tools are hardened to Rockwell
(Rc) 63 – 65 to withstand the heat and abrasion of
turning. If you happen to turn a HSS tool blue, the
hardness is reduced to about Rc 55 in the area of
the colour change so will dull fairly quickly but not
fail completely. If you turn carbon steel blue, it has
lost all its hardness in that area, so the only reasonable answer is to grind past that part. Tough to do
since grinding is the usual source of overheating in
the first place.
Grinding Wheels
Traditionally we have used vitrified wheels, that is,
wheels that are made up wholly of abrasives that
(Continued on page 13)
Editor’s Note: This is a recap of Ed’x excellent
demonstration at the May 2023 monthly meeting.
When purchasing gouges, insist on a clean, polished flute. Note the grooves in the flute in the
photo. These produce permanent built-in nicks in
the edge and require extensive and laborious honing to remove.

June 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 13
are bonded together. Their grades are determined
by the type of abrasive and the bonding agent.
These types of wheels are subject to cracking so it’s
imperative that they be “ring tested” before installation and after any time they are struck in a way
that may cause a crack. Ring test by holding the
wheel with your index finger in the mounting hole
and strike it with a piece of wood or plastic tool
handle. It should have a distinct and clear ring. If
it’s a dead thump it is cracked and needs to be discarded since it will blow apart when run up to
speed.
Vitrified grinding wheels are not multi purpose. Rather, they are designed for specific uses depending
on the abrasive and bonding strength. Gray stones
are general duty wheels with tough bonding agent
so they will tend to run “hot” and burn your tools
because they don’t “shed” their abrasive bits easily. Wheels that shed their abrasives readily tend to
run cooler. Blue stones are ideal for sharpening
woodturning tools. White stones are ideal for flat
edge tools (i.e. bench chisels or plane irons) but
break down rapidly under point contact from gouges. So, not so great for all the gouges we sharpen.
Vitrified wheels need to be trued and cleaned
often. When there is black evident, the wheel is
clogged with steel detritus and won’t cut well at
all. These wheels are usually out of balance and
can often be balanced by counter rotating one
against the other so that the set runs true. If that is
unsuccessful, balance weights are available. Vibration in your grinder is a huge detriment to a successful grind. Common grits are 80 and 120.
CBN wheels are a relatively new addition to our
sharpening arsenal. They are typically metal bodies
(usually steel) with Cubic Boron Nitride crystals
electroplated to the outer rim and varying degrees
of widths on the sides. Typically, they come in 80,
180 and 300 grits. Six hundred grit was produced
for a while but is rarely available now. Usually, they
are balanced (or stated that they didn’t require it)
and if they are not, don’t buy them. Contrary to
some uninformed opinions, it is possible to grind
high carbon steel tools using CBN. The important
thing to understand is that only hardened high carbon steel should be used. Mild steel (angle iron,
flat bar, etc.) will clog the wheels much like nonferrous metals on vitrified wheels.
Typically, it is understood that a minimum of 6”
diameter vitrified wheels should be used since a
tighter arc on the bevel tends to weaken the edge.
When you trim a 6” vitrified wheel to much less
than 6” then they need to be replaced (5 ¾” ?).
Eight-inch vitrified wheels can be trimmed many
times so are a better bargain overall but still should
be replaced once they are smaller than 6” diameter. From this, it is reasonable to get 6” diameter
CBN wheels since they never need to be trimmed.
It is common for people to have an 80 and 180 grit
wheel. One thing to consider is that the 80-grit
wheel is only necessary when shaping a new profile
(cuts faster and cooler). Considering that you usually only do that once on the life of a tool, an 80grit wheel is not that necessary. My recommendation is to get a singe 180 at first then a second
sometime later (one wheel on a grinder is not a
problem). An 80-grit vitrified wheel can be used
temporarily for shaping – or go over to a buddy’s
place to shape your new tool. Ideally, get an 80-grit
CBN – but later.
Remember that two 8” wheels will require more
than a ¾ hp grinder.
Grinding Jigs
Some sort of jig to make a controlled grind is a
huge advantage. Although it is possible to grind
freehand it takes a long time to learn, and a lot of
good steel disappears unnecessarily in that process. Most rests that come with grinders are inadequate, so for that reason alone the purchase of
some sort of grinding jig is almost a necessity. Two
advantages in having a means of making repeatable grinds are the savings in steel not ground away
and you are stepping back to the lathe with exactly
the same tool. Remember that the jig doesn’t create the profile for you. You still have to learn to
create that shape.
There are many setting gauges available for repeating rest angles and distances but once you determine that a certain setting is to your liking, it’s a
(Continued from page 12)
(Continued on page 14)

June 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 14
simple matter to make a pattern out of scrap
wood. The accuracy of setting the various angles on
any tool is not so important to cut wood. A few degrees one way or another isn’t that significant.
However, consistently setting the same angle reduces the amount of steel removed after changing
settings when resharpening.
Honing
Honing is something that is considered “part of the
deal” when sharpening flat woodworking tools but
somehow has become unnecessary in turning
tools. It is my observation that turners can be impatient so when it comes to sharpening, “close
counts” has become the norm.
To me, a cutting edge isn’t finished until is has been
ground, honed and stropped. I will admit that I
have gone straight from the grinder to the lathe,
but I had no expectations of a long-lasting edge nor
a finely cut surface.
I typically hone with a small hand-held 1200 grit
hone commonly available at KMS, Lee Valley and
probably other tools stores. I have a “credit card”
type hone but I prefer the smaller one because I
feel I have more control with that one. It’s imperative that you hone the heel and the cutting edge
equally to maintain the integrity of the bevel. Honing only the cutting edge produces a new bevel
that’s only a few thousandths of an inch wide,
therefore lifting the cutting edge off the wood. If
you use a credit card style, be careful to keep most
of the hone below the heel. It’s very easy to rock
the card because of the width. If most of the card is
above the cutting edge it will tend to hone the
cutting edge only.
I typically hone only the bevel (as long as the flute
has been polished). Rather than honing both sides,
I draw the edge through end grain hardwood
(maple works) to remove the now-weakened burr.
Usually honing the other side does that but why
mess up a nicely polished flute? Now that the bulk
of the burr (sometimes referred to as a “wire edge”
in sharpening jargon) is gone it’s time to strop.
I use water with a drop of dish detergent when
honing to keep the hone clean. At the moment I’m
trying Windex (YouTube vid) and it works well but
not better than water/detergent. The water is free
so when the Windex runs out, that’s it.
Stropping (and a bit on bench stones)
As a result of a couple of really good questions during the demonstration, I did a deep dive into both
stropping and bench stones. As a result, I have
made a couple of changes to the way I have been
stropping (and sharpening) for as long as I can remember.
First, I learned that my green wax/compound bar is
supposed to be 3 to 5 microns Chromium oxide but
those types of wax bars typically have random grits
up to 30 microns, thus rendering the smaller adjacent abrasives ineffective. The wax medium also
tends to clump causing further ineffectiveness.
I found that stropping compounds are available in a
paste form that is quite creamy and you spread
them on the leather with your finger resulting in a
more even application. Also, the abrasives are
more consistent, so when you get 2 – 3 micron
paste (equal to 8000 – 10,000 grit), you only get 23 micron abrasive. After some research I settled on
Trend brand that has a diamond abrasive. Perhaps
because of the diamond abrasive and perhaps because of the consistent size – or both – it cuts way
faster, so stropping is far more effective. It’s also
fine enough that the smooth side of the leather
holds an adequate amount. I’m very happy with
that little change.
Aside from turning tools, I hate to admit it, but I do
have some flat woodworking tools. These require
sharpening on bench stones. I was asked if I had
ever used “water stones” and the answer was “sort
of”. I recalled buying one and realized I would have
to totally convert from oil stones and the whole
regimen was going to be very expensive. In addition, water stones need to be trued often because
they are so soft, requiring even more “accessories”.
As a result of my recent research, I learned about
diamond “stones”. One of their advantages is that
they are very flat and don’t require truing (some of
my oil stones are so old that they require truing as
well). I got pretty excited when I realized I could
(Continued from page 13)
(Continued on page 15)

June 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 15
get one double sided diamond stone to do everything I needed (recently I also inherited an excellent 5000 grit diamond stone but that’s just
frosting on the cake). I got a “kit” from Woodworker Specialties that includes a double-sided stone
with 300 and 1200 grit with the proper honing fluid
and a couple other bits and bobs). Between that
diamond stone and the diamond stropping paste I
had all my bench chisels and plane irons flattened
on the back with a mirror finish and deadly sharp
edges in one afternoon. Now with the backs done,
sharpening will take no time at all.
I use water/detergent to clean my hone for my
turning tools (because it’s really cheap to replace),
but it’s important to note that for diamond stones,
proper synthetic honing fluid should be used. It
prevents rusting of the parent plate and unnecessary wear. It’s not expensive and it goes a long
way.
Jeweler’s Loop
The best tool you can get is get a 30X Jeweler’s
loop to examine your cutting edges. I’ve learned
more about what I do – or don’t do – to a cutting
edge than ever before with that tool. They are
cheap on Amazon.
Note that my photos were taken with a 15X lens so
30X really shows you what’s what.
Cutting Tools
With cutting tools in general, it’s best to have one,
clean facet the full length and breadth of the bevel.
Careful motions on the grinder are the key to
achieving that. Use your body rather than just your
arms – just like when you are turning. Although it is
commonly understood that one can step from the
grinder straight to the lathe, I believe that honing/
stropping is a necessary step in not only making a
(Continued from page 14)
(Continued on page 16)
Bevel ground with a 180-grit wheel. Note the
rough burr.
Honed with a 1200 grit hone. Note the remaining
burr. This is taken off easily by drawing it through
end grain hardwood. Also note the heel and
cutting edge are honed equally.
Stropped edge. Note the wavy appearance of the
edge due to the grooves in the
poorly ground flute apparent on the far side.

June 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 16
sharper, longer lasting edge, but in the end saves
time by not having to go back to the grinder so
often. I typically get at least two extra hone/strops
out of each grind so that’s two trips to the grinder
replaced by a quick hone and strop (or sometimes
just a quick strop) right at the lathe. Additionally, a
sharper edge requires much less sanding and much
less scraping since it’s easier to pick up a finer cut
with a deadly sharp tool when “tweaking” a shape.
And we all know a cut is easier to sand than the
finest scrape.
Should you prefer not to hone your tools, the skew
is one tool that you must hone because it has two
bevels and is used with either side against the
wood depending on the direction of the cut. If
there is a grinder burr on one side, the tool will not
cut if that side is against the wood. If you don’t believe me, try it.
A relief angle is a good thing to add to a grind because it makes the width of the bevel smaller than
the original, making it easier to control the tool in
certain situations. Also, less heat is produced
which reduces the breakdown of the cutting edge.
The resulting width of the bevel is your choice and
will likely evolve over time. Note that this is not the
same as a “secondary” bevel that is applied to the
cutting edge of a bevel. Rather, it is the removal of
material from the back or heel of the bevel. I use
an addition block in my gouge jig, but this is easily
done freehand since the relief bevel doesn’t affect
the true bevel.
Scraping Tools
The bevel(s) on all scraping tools, whether standard or negative rake, are simply to provide clearance between the tool and the wood, so your preference prevails. I usually grind my standard scrapers at 70° and my negative rake tools at 30° per
side which is the same as one of my skews (saving
an additional setting I don’t have to remember).
It is possible to use the grinder burr to do the
cutting but again, I prefer not to use that. As shown
in the photos, the grinder burr is very rough and is
only “stacked” on the tool rather than part of the
tool. As a result, it makes a rough cut and doesn’t
last very long. I use a handle holding a 1/8” carbide
rod (Dremel tool shank) to burnish a very sharp
and tough cutting edge on both my standard and
negative rake scrapers.
(Continued from page 15)
(Continued on page 17)
Scraper with a rough burr from the grinder
Clean, solid burr after honing and burnishing

June 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 17
After grinding either one, I hone the burr away so
that the tool has a clean edge. I then rub the burnishing tool at an angle to the tool to force the
edge up into a tooth by rubbing it back and forth
several times. A drop of oil helps things along. I’ve
learned to make lots of lighter passes rather than
trying to crush the edge over with only a couple of
passes. It’s far more effective than a grinder burr
and you have to be careful to NOT make the edge
too aggressive. It’s possible to re-burnish a couple
times on negative rake scrapers honing before regrinding, but the standard scrapers need to be reground every time. I’ve watched Mike Hoslaluk
hone the grinder burr away with a diamond hone
then use the tiny burr from the last hone on the
ground face as the cutting burr. I’ve tried it and it’s
very quick and very effective but not long-lasting.
Final Note
If any one tip will help more than any other, it’s to
sharpen before the tool gets dull. Your overall time
sharpening will be reduced, turning will be physically easier and your tool control will be far more
effective. At the risk of being repetitive, if you hone
and strop, a quick strop before it’s dull keeps you
in the game with no time lost at all.

Further reflections on the new woodturner’s adventure I’m on fills me with gratitude of the community of people who have helped me and been

do it again…”it” being whatever project, skill I happened to be doing at the time…to do it again, and
again, and again. Then to compare, refine, and do
it again, but with safety constantly in mind. Bruce

Diana asked to give a bit of my background including how I got into turning/woodworking. As with
all stories, it is long and a bit convoluted. It began
when I was about 6. My father gave me a jackknife
and a pocket hone and showed me how to use
them. His advice was a dull knife will cut you, not a
sharp one. I then took my newly sharpened knife
and proceeded to carve my initials into my school
desk top. Needless to say, I got caught. The result
was 2 weeks after school sanding that desk. I
learned to hate sanding at an early age but I
learned a new skill. Since then I have developed
loads of methods to make it less painful.
I grew up in a mountain town where the only thing
to do was to run across logs in the local mill log
pond and fish. I was introduced to the chainsaw at
about 12 when my boss on a ranch told me to take
an old Pioneer saw and cut down an oak tree for
fire wood. What a job, he never told me it had to
be sharpened. Don’t know why I am still alive.
These introductions to woodworking eventually led
me to study forestry and wood science and technology in university. In addition to growing trees
they taught us how to fall them and tear apart
wood with axes, saws, grinders and chemicals then
to find ways to put the pieces back together as new
products. This was the basis of my career.
The natural spinoff was my attraction to working
with wood as a hobby. My first major project was
building a stereo cabinet from Giant Sequoia on my
wife’s kitchen table with a handsaw, Skilsaw and
wood plane. This was followed by renovating 3
houses and building lots more furniture to fill
them. Of course, these required more tools and,
being cheap, I looked for good used tools at flea
markets, pawn shops and auctions. The result is my
present shop which is a collection of old tools,
some dating to the 1800’s.
I first became interested in turning wood over 30
years ago as a means of making small items for
other projects and honey dippers to go with my

bowls is the best way to develop basic skills. I
found I loved making these and prefer turning
bowls and practical items, especially live edge, to
more detailed art. I hope this will change as I develop more skills. My finish of choice is Minwax fast
dry poly. When mixed with thinners and applied
with different techniques, wipe on poly finishes can
range from an oil look to a high quality French
polish. It is also easy to work with and very forgiving.

2023 Shop CrawlsBy Steve Fairbairn
Summer Shop Crawls are back! Shop crawls, for
the uninitiated, are essentially an open house at
your workshop for other members to visit.
Other than a really good excuse to clean your shop,
they are an excellent way to meet, socialize and
perhaps solicit advice from fellow members.
Attending a Shop Crawl gives you an opportunity to
see how others work and have customized their
own workspaces to make them more comfortable
and enjoyable to work in. I’ve never attending a
Shop Crawl without coming away with several
great tips and ideas to adapt to my own workshop.
Shop Crawls are typically a half-day affair on a
weekend, either morning or afternoon (but could
be all day). Some folks put out coffee and/or
snacks but it is not required or expected.
If you want to show off your shop but don’t have
weekends available or just don’t like the idea of
having people in your space, you could instead record a virtual shop crawl on your smartphone as you
take us on a narrated tour of your shop. Your video will be posted on our YouTube channel for only
members to view and can be removed anytime at
your request. For examples, check out our August
2021 GVWG Virtual Shop Crawls at https://
youtu.be/JQNXvMrkoAE.
To schedule your physical Shop Crawl, or to submit
the recording of your Virtual Shop Crawl, contact
Steve Fairbairn at editor@gvwg.ca. We will send
out invitations to the membership as we receive
the appropriate information.

the GVWG and you’re done. The easiest way to do
this is to go online to: https://www.kmstools.com/
group-rewards and fill in a short form. In doing so,

from better pricing on their full line of products. As
a friendly reminder if you are already a KMS Club

Safety Guidelines for WoodturningYou mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility
 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock
(Continued on page 38)

June 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 38
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage.
